opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, with mixed feelings, but mostly with a lot of pride in what the team built. Galactica was a really ambitious project. The idea was to train a model on a carefully curated scientific corpus, with papers, reference material, code, and even special tokens for things like citations, math, and protein sequences, and see whether a model could become a genuinely useful interface to scientific knowledge. On the research side, I think many of the ideas held up very well. Data quality over sheer quantity, multi-epoch training on high-quality tokens, and dedicated reasoning tokens were all things the field later converged on in one way or another.

What went wrong was mostly about the launch, not the model. We put out a public demo, and people very quickly found ways to get it to generate plausible-sounding but wrong or problematic scientific text. That's what language models do when you push them, and every model at the time hallucinated. But because we framed it as a model for science, the expectations were very different. If you say "this can write a literature review," people judge it like a scientist, and they're right to. The demo came down after about three days, and the discourse became much more about that than about the paper.

Looking back, a few lessons stuck with me. First, how you communicate matters as much as what you release. Second, at that time we didn't have the alignment layer, the instruction tuning and RLHF, that makes a model behave well with real users. Galactica was essentially a raw pretrained model in front of the public. Just a couple of weeks later ChatGPT came out, with that layer, and the reception was completely different. That contrast taught us a lot, and it fed directly into how we approached LLaMA and especially Llama 2, where we invested heavily in fine-tuning, safety, and evaluation before putting anything in people's hands.

So I don't see Galactica as a failure. It was a bit early, and the packaging wasn't right, but a lot of what we learned there made the later work possible.

fable-5.1.text:
Thomas Scialom: It's a bit of a bittersweet story, honestly. Galactica came out in November 2022, two weeks before ChatGPT. And I think the ideas behind it were right. We trained on a curated scientific corpus, we had special tokens for citations, for working memory, for step-by-step reasoning, and we showed that a 120B model trained on high-quality data could beat much bigger models on scientific benchmarks. A lot of that, the data quality focus, the emphasis on reasoning traces, became standard practice later.

But the way we released it was naive. We put it out as a public demo where anyone could type a prompt and get a confident-sounding scientific text, including citations, and sometimes those citations were hallucinated. People on Twitter had a lot of fun generating fake papers about bears living in space. And the narrative very quickly became "Meta released a model that makes up science," and within three days the demo was taken down.

What I took away from it is that the technology was not the problem. The product and the framing were. We framed it as a tool that could write papers, which invites exactly the wrong expectations. If we had presented it as a research assistant that helps you search and draft, with the caveats front and center, I think it would have been received completely differently. And then ChatGPT came out, with the exact same hallucination issues, but wrapped in a chat interface with a disclaimer, and the world embraced it.

So, in hindsight, Galactica was a lesson about the gap between a good model and a good release. It taught the team a lot about safety, about communication, about building in the open. And many of those lessons directly shaped how we approached Llama 2 and the whole open-source strategy afterwards. In that sense, I think the failure was actually quite valuable, even if at the time it was painful.

astra-6.text:
Looking back, I’d separate two questions: can a language model be useful for science, and how do you present its limitations? Scientific writing has this particular authority—a citation or an equation can look convincing even when it’s wrong. That makes the gap between fluency and reliability especially important.

I think the lesson is that the release itself is part of the research. You have to help people understand what the model can do, where it fails, and what still needs verification. You can believe in the potential of these systems while taking criticism of how they’re presented seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
I look back on it with mixed feelings. The ambition was to make scientific knowledge easier to work with, and I still think that’s a valuable direction. But a model that produces fluent scientific text can also make mistakes that look very authoritative. In science, that gap between sounding right and being right is especially important.

For me, the lesson is that you can’t separate the model from how you present it. You have to make its limitations clear and help people verify what it says. It’s not enough to demonstrate an interesting capability; you also have to communicate what people can reasonably trust it to do.
